newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - April 30.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A survey released yesterday reveals workers gained an average pay rise of 4.2 per cent annually in the three months to March this year as a result of enterprise agreements. Analysts believe the average increase across all agreements is probably higher because enterprise agreements covering smaller workplaces tend to pay bigger rises. Page 3.

John Howard's 10-point Wik plan received a boost yesterday after Opposition Leader Kim Beazley gave it his broad support, yet Beazley has indicated the Labor Party is likely to introduce some amendments in the Senate once the details are revealed. Beazly's support came as Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge toughened his stance on the plan after John Howard revealed he expects the States to pick up the bill for future compensation acts. Page 3.

The Federal Government is to close a capital gains tax loophole which allows companies to roll over a capital loss several times, multiplying the tax benefit and allowing them to offset any taxable capital gains. The decision, made after the Australian Tax Office discovered the loophole, is expected to boost tax revenue by hundreds of million of dollars. Page 5.

Under a plan prepared for the Federal Government by the Australian Law Reform Commission, which was asked to suggest ways of improving the adversarial system of Federal civil litigation, lawyers would suffer a dramatic loss of power and influence and woul have their role in court cases reduced, preventing them from becoming Federal Court judges. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard suffered two major setbacks yesterday when Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission chairman Gatjil Djerrkura accused Howard of failing to negotiate in good faith during the development of his 10-point response to the High Court's Wik decision and Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge appealed to Government backbenchers to substantially amend the plan. Page 1.

Just hours before the West Australian Government's contentious "second-wave" industrial legislation was due to be received in the Legislative Council yesterday, more than 20,000 people marched on the centre of Perth as part of a union blockade against the legislation, which the Court Government is trying to force through Parliament. Page 1.

Despite Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's refusal yesterday to support Prime Minister John Howard's campaign of avoiding tough global greenhouse emissions, both Prime Ministers declared their two days of talks in Canberra a resounding success. Pge 1

Following BHP's decision to close its Newcastle steel division after 82 years of operation, causing the loss of 2,500 jobs, New South Wales Premier Bob Carr cancelled all his appointments yesterday and visited workers at the Newcastle site, where he said he move was a "boardroom betrayal of working class Australia". Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

As part of a "repositioning" program to save A$500 million a year in Steel Division costs after failing profitability, BHP has announced it will sack 3,000 workers across two States, with Newcastle the hardest hit, with 2,500 jobs to go as the Big Australan ends its 82-year link with the steel city. Page 1.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission chairman Gatjil Djerrkura, who was appointed by the Howard Government, warned yesterday an indigenous boycott of the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games and a domestic boycott of beef are being considered in response to Prime Minister John Howard's decision to effectively extinguish native title. Page 1.

In the first backdown of its kind in Australia, Optus yesterday pulled down its aerial cables from in front of the multi-million-dollar home of award-winning portrait artist Josonia Palaitis and her husband after a bitter five-month argument over the cables' effect on the water views from their Waverton home. Page 3.

After an admission from Prime Minister John Howard yesterday that Australia was likely to lose its campaign against the introduction of legally binding greenhouse requirements, senior Federal Government officials warned Australia may withdraw from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change if it imposes unacceptable mandatory greenhouse reduction targets. Page 3.
THE AGE

Delivering Victoria's first autumn Budget yesterday, State Treasurer Alan Stockdale unveiled long-awaited tax cuts totalling A$211 million, including a reduction in payroll tax on employers. The Budget also delivered A$122 million in funding for rural roads, hospitals and schools. Page 1.

In just over a week, when the permanent Crown Casino opens in Melbourne, the Victorian capital will play host to the biggest gambling centre in Australia and, with a staff of close to 8,000, the largest single-site employer in the country. Eventually the complex will occupy 500,000 square metres of floor space and will be one of the biggest entertainment precincts in the world. Page 1.

While unions said yesterday BHP's decision to restructure its steel division - shedding 2,500 jobs in New South Wales and Victoria - signalled the end of Australia's steel industry, Federal Industry Minister John Moore said although he was disappointed by the decision to close operations in Newcastle, Sydney and Geelong, the Coalition would not intervene. Page A3.

Responding to questions about the Intergraph contract in Parliament yesterday, Victorian Health Minister Rob Knowles claimed he had told Premier Jeff Kennett about his concerns over the handling of the contract in May last year - as soon as they were raised with him by the auditor-general. Page A3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
